text: I always think that the best way to combat the unwillingness of the commoner to actively engage in politics is to bring them to the commoner. People behave very differently when comparing communities to even just the town or city they live in. They behave to their neighbor much differently than someone a 15 minute drive from, and absolutely differently from someone they never see. story: This is the best explanation of gerrymandering you will ever see
text: PR mitigates Gerrymandering because it reduces the amount of "discardable" surplus votes. Imagine you have 100 single-winner districts that are each roughly 50/50 Dem/GOP, with the slight edge breaking 50/50, so that your legislature has 50 reps from each party. Now we redistrict to pack a bunch of Dems from the GOP-majority districts into one super-Dem district, shaving down their margins in numerous districts. We could conceivable get 99 GOP reps even though the population is 50/50 Dem/GOP. That super-Dem district "discards" or "wastes" 50% of the votes of the Dems inside it, because they're surplus votes in excess of what they need to win the district. Now imagine you switch to 20 5-winner districts elected with PR. The Dems could win all five seats with conceivably 83.3% of the vote (5 candidates getting 16.6% each means they get all the votes). So the most you can possibly wast is 16.7% of the votes instead of 50%. > It only replaces districts with parties No. Most PR systems still have districts. Exceptions like Israel, where the whole country is one big district, tend to be the poster children of PR gone wrong. Plus there are PR systems where you vote for candidates, not parties. Single Transferable Vote in Australia's Senate is an example. You just rank the candidates (although many voters blindly follow the guidance of their preferred party).
